sources.title: PLACEHOLDER — History of modern Greek cookery

intro.text: Layers of fried aubergine and minced lamb or beef cooked with tomato, sealed under a thick béchamel and baked until the top is browned and set.
The béchamel-topped form is associated with Greece; the same name covers quite different dishes in the Balkans, Turkey and the Levant.
It is cut into thick slices and served warm, once it has rested enough to hold its layers.

about.text: The béchamel crust is usually credited to Nikolaos Tselementes, the Greek cookery writer whose manuals of the 1910s and 1920s brought French techniques into Greek home kitchens.
Older dishes recorded under the same name were layered or stewed without it.
In Greece it is more often a dish for Sundays, name days and tavernas than for weeknights, since each layer is cooked separately before the dish is assembled.
Versions with potato or courgette, alongside or instead of aubergine, are common, and meatless versions are made for Lent.

places.explanation: Greek cookbooks treat the béchamel-topped form as the standard version.

chapters.title: A French crust in a Greek manual
chapters.label: Tselementes' cookery manuals give a moussaka finished with béchamel, the form now associated with Greece.
chapters.scope_note: Reported in secondary sources; the manuals were not inspected directly, so the first edition with béchamel is not fixed.
